title: Your Newborn's First Days
learningGoals: Recognize how a healthy newborn often looks, from head shape to skin
Know what's normal for newborn breathing and sleep
Understand early weight loss, and when babies regain it
Know how a newborn's poop changes in the first week
Understand jaundice basics, and when it's checked

review.notes: Drafted 2026-10-18 as lesson 5.1, the first lesson of Module 5 (Feeding and Newborn Care) in course order. Covers what's normal; warning signs and when to call are taught in lesson 6.3, and this lesson points there rather than repeating them. Safe sleep is in lesson 5.5. Sources were found by web search only; this session could not open the pages, so every new source needs to be opened and confirmed. For the reviewer: head molding rounding out within a few days, soft spots that may pulse, and milia clearing in 2 to 3 weeks follow the AAP head and appearance pages; swollen breasts or genitals and a little vaginal discharge or spotting from the mother's hormones are common newborn findings not confirmed in these exact pages; the breathing slide repeats lesson 6.3's reviewed wording and adds that short pauses can be normal, not confirmed word for word; about 16 to 17 hours of sleep a day follows an AAP page that gives about 17; early weight loss with birth weight regained by about 2 weeks follows the AAP first-month page, and the slide gives no percentage; the stool color changes (black and sticky, then greenish, then yellow and seedy for breastfed babies by about day 5) are standard teaching not confirmed word for word; the jaundice slide repeats lesson 6.3's call-back signs by reference and adds that jaundice is checked before discharge.

slides.heading: Your Newborn's First Days
onScreen: Module 5: Feeding and Newborn Care
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 5, Feeding and Newborn Care. Newborns can look and act in ways that surprise new parents. In this first lesson, we'll go over what's normal in the first days: how your baby may look, breathe, sleep, and grow, and what jaundice is. Knowing what's normal makes it easier to spot when something isn't.

visual.description: A new parent sitting in a hospital bed, gazing at their newborn wrapped in a blanket in their arms, while their partner leans in beside them, smiling. Exactly one baby. No pregnant belly. No readable writing.

slides.heading: How your newborn may look
onScreen: A cone-shaped or uneven head usually rounds out in a few days
Soft spots on the head are normal, and may pulse
Puffy eyes and face, and some swelling on the scalp
A white, waxy coating on the skin is a natural moisturizer
slides.narration: Many newborns don't look like the babies in pictures, and that's normal. A baby's skull is made of soft plates that shift to fit through the birth canal, so the head may look cone-shaped or uneven. It usually rounds out within a few days. There are two soft spots on the head, which are normal, and may gently pulse. The eyes and face may look puffy, and there may be some swelling on the scalp from birth. Some babies have a white, waxy coating on their skin, which is a natural moisturizer.

visual.description: A close, gentle view of a sleeping newborn wrapped in a blanket and held in a parent's arms, with a slightly elongated head, puffy eyelids, and a few tiny white spots on the nose. Calm and tender. Exactly one baby. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Newborn skin
onScreen: Tiny white bumps on the nose and cheeks (milia)
Blotchy red spots or newborn rash
Pink or bluish-gray birthmarks
Dry, peeling skin, especially on hands and feet
slides.narration: Newborn skin goes through a lot of changes. Tiny white bumps on the nose and cheeks, called milia, usually clear within two or three weeks. Blotchy red spots that come and go are common in the first days. Many babies have birthmarks, like pink patches on the eyelids or the back of the neck, or bluish-gray patches on the back or bottom. And dry, peeling skin, especially on the hands and feet, is normal too. Most of these fade on their own.

visual.description: Four simple icons with short labels for normal newborn skin: sparkles for tiny white bumps, a dotted circle for blotchy red spots, a palette for birthmarks, and a hand for peeling skin.

slides.heading: Other normal surprises
onScreen: Swollen breasts or genitals, from your hormones
A little vaginal discharge in baby girls
Hiccups, sneezes, and startles
Eyes that sometimes cross
slides.narration: A few other things can surprise new parents. Hormones from pregnancy can make a newborn's breasts or genitals look swollen for a while, in boys and girls, and baby girls may have a little white discharge, or even a few drops of blood, from the vagina. Hiccups, sneezes, and sudden startles are all normal. And a newborn's eyes may cross or wander at times, as the eye muscles get stronger. Ask your baby's doctor about anything that worries you.

visual.description: Four simple icons with short labels: a heart for hormone swelling, a droplet for a little discharge, a wind symbol for hiccups and sneezes, and an eye for eyes that cross.

question.prompt: Your newborn's head looks a little cone-shaped after a vaginal birth. What's most likely?
options: It's a sign of a serious problem
The soft skull plates shifted during birth, and it usually rounds out in a few days
question.explanation: A newborn's skull plates shift to fit through the birth canal, so the head may look cone-shaped. It usually rounds out within a few days.

slides.heading: Newborn breathing
onScreen: Breathing is faster than an adult's, and often uneven
Short pauses during sleep can be normal
Snuffly, noisy breathing through the nose is common
Struggling to breathe, or blue lips: call 911 (lesson 6.3)
slides.narration: Newborns breathe faster than adults, and their breathing is often uneven, especially in sleep. It may speed up, slow down, and pause briefly, for a few seconds, before starting again. Their noses are small, so snuffly, noisy breathing is common. Lesson 6.3 covers the warning signs in detail. Remember, if your baby is struggling to breathe, or their lips or face turn blue, call 911.

visual.description: A newborn sleeping on their back in a bare bassinet, in a fitted sheet only, while a parent sits beside the bassinet watching calmly. No pillows, blankets, bumpers, toys, or hat. Exactly one baby. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Newborn sleep
onScreen: About 16 to 17 hours a day, in short stretches
Waking often to feed, day and night
Days and nights mixed up at first
Always on the back, in their own sleep space (lesson 5.5)
slides.narration: Newborns sleep a lot, about 16 to 17 hours a day, but in short stretches. They wake often to feed, day and night, because their stomachs are small. Many have their days and nights mixed up at first, and that slowly sorts itself out over the first weeks. Ask your baby's doctor whether to wake your baby for feeds in the early days. And for every sleep, put your baby on their back, in their own safe sleep space, as you learned in the safe sleep lesson.

visual.description: Night time: a tired but smiling parent sitting in a chair beside a bare bassinet where their newborn sleeps on their back in a fitted sheet only, a small night light glowing. No pillows, blankets, bumpers, toys, or hat. Exactly one baby. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Weight in the first weeks
onScreen: Most babies lose some weight in the first days
Steady gains usually start around day 5
Most are back to birth weight by about 2 weeks
Your baby is weighed at each early checkup
slides.narration: Most babies lose some weight in the first days after birth, mostly extra fluid they were born with. That's expected. Steady gains usually start around day five, and most babies are back to their birth weight by about two weeks. Your baby will be weighed before you go home and at each early checkup, usually within a few days of leaving the hospital. Your baby's doctor will tell you if the weight loss is more than expected.

visual.description: Three stacked steps: the first days, some weight loss; around day 5, steady gains begin; by about 2 weeks, back to birth weight.

slides.heading: Diapers in the first week
onScreen: First 1 to 2 days: black, sticky poop (meconium)
Days 3 to 4: greenish-brown
By about day 5: yellow and seedy for breastfed babies
More wet diapers each day as feeding picks up
slides.narration: Diapers change a lot in the first week, and they're a good sign of how feeding is going. The first poops are black and sticky. This is called meconium. Around days three and four, they turn greenish-brown. By about day five, breastfed babies usually have yellow, seedy, loose poops, while formula-fed babies' poops are often tan and firmer. You'll also see more wet diapers each day as feeding picks up. Lesson 6.3 covers how many to expect, and when to call.

visual.description: Three stacked steps of stool color: black and sticky in the first days, greenish-brown around days 3 to 4, and yellow and seedy by about day 5 for breastfed babies.

slides.heading: Jaundice basics
onScreen: Many newborns look a little yellow in the first week
It usually starts on the face and moves down
Your baby is checked before going home and at the first checkup
Sunlight isn't a treatment; call if you're worried (lesson 6.3)
slides.narration: Many newborns look a little yellow in the first week. This is called jaundice. It happens because a newborn's body is still learning to clear a substance called bilirubin. The yellow usually starts on the face, and can move down the body. Your baby will be checked for jaundice before you go home, and again at the first checkup. Most jaundice clears on its own, but some babies need treatment with special lights. Don't put your baby in sunlight to treat it. Lesson 6.3 covers when to call.

visual.description: A nurse gently holding a small handheld skin-check device to a newborn's forehead as the baby lies in a hospital bassinet, while the parent watches beside it. Exactly one baby. No readable writing or numbers.

slides.heading: Questions for your baby's first checkup
onScreen: Anything about how your baby looks that you want checked
Questions about sleep, weight, or diapers
Who will be your baby's doctor
slides.narration: Your baby's first checkup is usually a few days after you go home. Think about what you'd like to ask. Is there anything about how your baby looks that you want checked? Questions about sleep, weight, or diapers? And have you chosen your baby's doctor yet? Save your questions to your Birth Readiness Brief.
slides.prompt: Write the questions you'd like to ask at your baby's first checkup, and who your baby's doctor will be.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: A cone-shaped head, puffy eyes, and skin spots are often normal
Breathing is fast and uneven; sleep comes in short stretches
Babies lose some weight, then regain it by about 2 weeks
Poop changes from black to yellow; jaundice is checked early
slides.narration: Let's recap. Newborns often have a cone-shaped head, puffy eyes, and skin spots that fade on their own. Their breathing is fast and uneven, and they sleep in short stretches, always on their back. Most babies lose some weight at first, then regain it by about two weeks. Poop changes from black and sticky to yellow, and jaundice is checked before you go home. Next up, a few review questions.

reviewQuiz.prompt: When are most babies back to their birth weight?
reviewQuiz.explanation: Most babies lose some weight in the first days, start gaining around day 5, and are back to their birth weight by about 2 weeks.

reviewQuiz.prompt: What do a newborn's first poops usually look like?
reviewQuiz.explanation: The first poops, called meconium, are black and sticky. They change to greenish-brown, then yellow for breastfed babies, over the first week.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Your baby looks a little yellow on day 3. What's a good step?
options: Know that jaundice is common, and call your baby's doctor if it's spreading, deep yellow, or you're worried
reviewQuiz.explanation: Jaundice is common in the first week and usually clears on its own. Sunlight isn't a treatment. Call if it's spreading, deep yellow or orange, or you're worried, as lesson 6.3 explains.
